paras: The killing of Bill Allen was the shooting by Chicago police of a Black waiter in a chicken coop near the North Halsted Street rail yards on Sunday afternoon, December 3, 1882, after a city-wide manhunt. Allen was accused of killing Officer Clarence E. Wright four days earlier, and the most widely printed dispatch said police shot him after he threw up his hands and offered to surrender. A crowd of thousands then tried to hang his body, and a coroner's jury exonerated the two officers who shot him.

Allen, also called Joe Dahlman and known as 'the Colonel', had worked as a waiter on Pullman cars of the Chicago & Northwestern railroad. According to a long Chicago account, he and a cook, James Smead, were discharged on a charge of stealing provisions and blamed a fellow Black waiter, William Jones, whom Allen was accused of striking three times on the head with a hammer on the morning of November 29. That evening Detective John Fletcher, Officers Wright and T. Foley and a guide went to Allen's room at 37 West Washington Street, where Allen was said to have fired through the opened door, killing Wright, and escaped.
The police searched the city and neighboring towns for days; at Kalamazoo a Black cook, Charles Almon, was arrested as Allen and released as the wrong man.

On the afternoon of December 3 the police learned that Allen was hiding behind 134 North Halsted Street, and a squad went out, in the dispatch's words, under orders that he 'must be taken dead or alive—dead preferred.' Policeman Patrick Mulvahill reached the house first with his brother and was shot over the left eye, and Allen fled into the Northwestern and Pan Handle railroad yards.

In the Wood County Reporter's narrative, a boy following the officers tilted a dry-goods box in a chicken coop by the Pan Handle track and found Allen under it. Officer Wheeler shut the coop door and fired through it; Allen called out 'I's got enough,' and Wheeler fired twice more. As the crowd, now numbering thousands, rushed the body with cries of 'Hang him,' two more shots were fired into it, and someone tied a clothes-line around the neck while officers pulled the other way.

A patrol wagon forced its way through the crowd on the order of the Desplaines street captain, and the body was carried to the station with the rope still around its neck. When the crowd outside shouted 'lynch him!' and refused to believe Allen was dead, police laid the body on a board at the window and had people file past for two hours.

The chief of police discharged Officers Fletcher and Foley, who had been with Wright on November 29, for cowardice. At the inquest on Allen the coroner's jury found that he died of gunshot wounds from Officers John Wheeler and John Reid 'in the discharge of their duty' and exonerated them. Jones died at the County Hospital on December 9, and Mulvahill was in critical condition after a second operation found a fractured skull. No report of Mulvahill's recovery or of any further inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

No Chicago paper's own report is in the coverage; the story spread through a Western Associated Press dispatch and a St. Paul Globe special telegram. The same dispatch drew opposite headlines: the Omaha Bee ran 'BLACK MAN BORED. A Murderous Darkey Riddled with Bullets,' while the National Republican wrote 'How the Chicago Policemen Killed a Desporado After His Surrender' and the Benton Weekly Record 'Lynched by Chicago Police.'

Brief items in Maine, New Hampshire, Ohio and Iowa reduced the story to a 'negro desperado' riddled with bullets; an Omaha Bee editorial paragraph later said Allen had been 'assassinated after surrendered.'

Accounts of the final moments differ: the wire dispatch has Allen leaving a hen coop with his hands up, the Globe telegram has him firing into the crowd before Sergeant Wheeler shot him through a shed window, and the Wood County narrative has him shot through the closed coop door. A New Haven dispatch instead described a gunfight at a friend's house, and the date of Wright's killing varies across reports, though the same-night wire dated it November 29.

reader.title: Killing of Bill Allen
bases: Chicago police officers, hunting Allen for killing an officer, shot him dead in a chicken coop or shed while a large crowd joined the search and then tried to hang his body (A8, A9, A23, A27).
The Western Associated Press dispatch, a separate Globe special telegram, a long Chicago narrative and the coroner's verdict all agree that police shot Allen dead on Dec. 3 (A8, A9, A23, A27).

accounts.label: Western Associated Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Police had orders to take Allen 'dead or alive, dead preferred'; after shots into the hen coop he came out, threw up his hands and offered to surrender, but the police refused and riddled him with bullets.

accounts.label: Globe special telegram
accounts.gist: Allen leaped from a dry-goods box, fired into the crowd, ran, and was brought to bay in a shed on West Kinzie Street, where Sergeant Wheeler shot him four times through a window.

accounts.label: Long Chicago narrative (Wood County Reporter)
accounts.gist: A boy found Allen under a dry-goods box in a chicken coop; Wheeler shut the door and fired through it as Allen called out 'I's got enough', fired twice more, and two more shots were fired into the body as the crowd rushed in.

accounts.label: New Haven dispatch
accounts.gist: A little girl reported Allen at a friend's house; he fought the officers who surrounded it, wounding Policeman 'Melville' in the back, and was given six mortal wounds; the mob tried to seize the dying man and lynch him.

accounts.label: Weekly summary
accounts.gist: Allen was found in a coal-box and the police opened fire without summoning him to surrender.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Allen died of gunshot wounds from Officers Wheeler and Reid acting in the discharge of their duty; they were exonerated.

framing.detail: The Omaha Bee headlined 'BLACK MAN BORED. A Murderous Darkey Riddled with Bullets' while printing the dispatch's account of a refused surrender.
The St. Paul Globe's 'The Murderous Bill Allen Killed' called him a 'villian' who fell 'with a yell of rage' and likened the body's display to 'a day at the circus'.
The National Republican headlined how police 'Killed a Desporado After His Surrender'.
The Benton Weekly Record ran the dispatch as 'Lynched by Chicago Police'.
An Omaha Bee editorial paragraph called Allen 'a very common murderer' who 'was assassinated after surrendered', mocking the force it took to kill him.
Weekly summaries carried one-line notices of the 'negro desperado' riddled with bullets.

conflicts.note: The Wood County narrative is the fullest and names the boy, the coop and the door; the wire dispatch's surrender account was the most widely reprinted. The inquest, as reported, gave no detail on the shooting.
The same-night Nov. 29 wire (A1) is the best evidence for Nov. 29.
